For each flagged item, rule whether the key's answer is uniquely defensible from the evidence (key-uniquely-defensible), whether two answers are defensible (ambiguous), or whether the key is wrong (key-wrong). If not uniquely defensible, propose the smallest change to the case evidence or the key that would make exactly one answer defensible.

3	Answer semantics:
4	- hypothesis: "supported" = the evidence, taken together, supports the claim more than its rivals; "contradicted" = the evidence counts against it; "unknown" = the evidence does not discriminate, so the claim is live but unestablished.
5	- edge (a claimed link from one condition to another): "causal" = the evidence supports a causal link (for example temporal order plus mechanism plus covariation with the main rival ruled out, a natural experiment, or an intervention result); "association-only" = they co-occur or correlate in the evidence but causation is not established; "contradicted" = evidence counts against the link; "unknown" = evidence is insufficient even to show association.
6	- action: "preferred" = among the best next actions given the evidence; "acceptable" = reasonable but not among the best; "premature" = could be right if a still-unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed, but committing now is not justified; "harmful" = likely to worsen outcomes, suppress information, punish the wrong party, or disable a protective control.
7	- sufficiency (item SUFF): is the evidence sufficient to commit to the action you rank highest, where that action is substantive rather than merely evidence-gathering? "sufficient" or "insufficient". Concluding that no intervention is warranted counts as a substantive decision.
8	- Items with asOfStage set must be answered using only evidence whose stage is at or before that stage.

361	CASE OD2-HO-INTERACT-2 (INTERACT, organizational): Larkspur Community Food Network: regular volunteers drifting away
362	Setting: Larkspur Community Food Network is a fictional regional food-relief nonprofit with four pantry sites (Millbrook, Dock Street, Westgate and Quarry Lane). It relies on about 420 regular volunteers who sort, pack and serve food, including an after-school meals programme for minors at every site. In spring 2026 it introduced a self-scheduling app (RotaWeave) and an annual background-check renewal. After losing a foundation grant, it also eliminated three site coordinator posts. Between March and August the number of active regular volunteers fell sharply, and the board meets on 30 September.
363	Presenting request: The executive director wants an independent view of why regular volunteers have stopped coming and what Larkspur should do. She intends to recommend cancelling the RotaWeave contract at the 30 September board meeting unless the evidence points elsewhere.
364	INITIAL EVIDENCE
365	E1 [stage S1] Mara Ellison, Executive Director, memo to reviewer, 2 September 2026 (leadership-account): Our active regular volunteers fell from 421 in March to 295 in August, the worst drop in our eleven years. I have personally taken about a dozen calls from long-serving volunteers who are furious about RotaWeave, the scheduling app we adopted this spring. At the 30 September board meeting I intend to recommend cancelling the RotaWeave contract and going back to the paper rosters that served us for a decade. One board member also thinks Commonplate Volunteers, a new group that opened on 16 June, is poaching our people. I need an independent view of what happened and what we should do before that meeting.
366	E2 [stage S1] Larkspur project and policy change log (extract) (change-record): RotaWeave rollout plan (approved 12 Feb): Millbrook pilot go-live 3 March; Dock Street, Westgate and Quarry Lane go-live 14 April. Basic tier: next week's shifts released to all volunteers every Thursday at 18:00; three staff admin seats; 3-year term, $38,000; early-termination fee $14,000. Policy change (adopted 20 Jan): annual background-check renewal for all regular volunteers, required by the county after-school meals contract and by our insurer for any shift serving minors. Renewal deadline 30 April; volunteers not renewed are deactivated on 1 May until they complete it.
367	E3 [stage S1] Finance memo to staff, 22 April 2026 (financial-record): After the loss of the Pellham Foundation operating grant ($171,000), the following savings take effect on 1 May. The site coordinator posts at Dock Street, Westgate and Quarry Lane are eliminated (3.0 FTE, $148,000 annualised), and volunteer oversight at those three sites moves to the regional operations manager. The Millbrook coordinator post is kept because the county senior-meals contract funds it separately. The remaining savings come from reduced van leasing. We recognise this places extra load on site lead volunteers and thank them for their flexibility.
368	E4 [stage S1] Email from Tobias Wren, Director of Operations and sponsor of the RotaWeave project, to the Executive Director, 28 August 2026 (manager-account): Mara, before the board blames RotaWeave, look at Millbrook. It has been on the app since March, longer than any other site, and its numbers are fine. The slide starts in May, not April. On 1 May we deactivated 23 regulars who hadn't finished their background-check renewal, and plenty more told me the renewal portal was a nightmare. I think the renewal drove people off whether or not they finished it. Cancelling RotaWeave would cost $14k and throw away the attendance data we've finally got for funders. Tobias
369	E5 [stage S1] Volunteer database, board-pack extract (system-record): Definition: an active regular is a volunteer with 3 or more shifts in the prior 60 days. Org-wide month-end counts: Jan 409, Feb 414, Mar 421, Apr 415, May 384, Jun 345, Jul 315, Aug 295. Renewal deadline: 23 regulars were deactivated on 1 May for an incomplete background-check renewal. Of these, 21 completed it and were reactivated by 31 May; the other 2 have since moved away. Site-level counts are not part of the standard board pack.
370	E6 [stage S1] Volunteer pulse survey summary, February and June 2026 (anonymous-staff-survey): Anonymous link sent to all regulars. Overall satisfaction (1–5): February mean 4.2 (n=236); June mean 3.5 (n=198). The lowest-scoring item in June was 'ease of getting the shifts I want' at 3.0, down from 4.1. Follow-up: 61 June respondents chose to give their names and were matched to activity records. Of those who scored overall satisfaction at 2 or below, 7 of 19 (37%) were inactive by August, against 4 of 42 (10%) of the rest. Site is not recorded.
371	CATALOGUE (full contents)
372	C1 [stage S1] RotaWeave uptime and support-ticket summary, April–August 2026 - RotaWeave customer success team (vendor-account): Platform uptime was 99.8%, with two incidents (14 May and 9 July) of under 40 minutes each, both outside shift-release windows. There were 46 support tickets: 21 password resets, 11 SMS notification settings, 8 export questions and 6 other. No open defects affect booking. Adoption: 92% of active volunteers at live sites logged in at least once in August. Account manager's note: 'Larkspur is one of our smoothest Basic-tier deployments. Columns run March to August. Millbrook (RotaWeave since 3 Mar; coordinator kept): 118, 117, 116, 114, 112, 111. Dock Street (RotaWeave since 14 Apr; coordinator post ended 1 May): 112, 110, 96, 78, 64, 55. Westgate (RotaWeave since 14 Apr; coordinator post ended 1 May): 105, 103, 88, 70, 58, 49. Quarry Lane (coordinator post ended 1 May; RotaWeave not live because the kiosk tablets were never delivered, go-live moved to 6 Oct; the lead volunteer keeps the paper standing roster): 86, 85, 84, 83, 81, 80. The background-check deadline applied in the same way at all four sites.
374	C3 [stage S1] Exit-survey responses from volunteers flagged inactive, May–August 2026 - Automated exit email, responses coded by a volunteer-services intern (document): Sent to 141 volunteers flagged inactive; 13 responded (9%). Reasons, coded from free text: busy/other commitments 4, health 2, moved away 1, 'changes at the pantry' 3, prefer not to say 3. The site field was optional and left blank in 11 responses. Share referred by a corporate partner: 6%, 9%, 7%, 5%.
377	C6 [stage S1] Interview with the regional operations manager, 3 September 2026 - Imran Castell, Regional Operations Manager (covering Dock Street, Westgate and Quarry Lane since 1 May) (manager-account): 'I can't be at three sites, so I manage from the RotaWeave dashboard. rulings.explanation: The key's answer, 'acceptable', is the only one that fits the definitions. 'Harmful' means likely to worsen outcomes, suppress information, punish the wrong party, or disable a protective control. A4 does none of these to the outcome in question. Under the supported joint cause (H3), taking either ingredient away removes the fall. Quarry Lane in C2 had its coordinator cut but no app, kept a paper standing roster, and stayed stable at 86->80. So going back to paper rosters at Dock Street and Westgate would probably stop regulars losing their slots, which improves retention. Millbrook ran on paper rosters for a decade before the app and still has its coordinator, so nothing suggests its retention would suffer. The blind solver gives two reasons for 'harmful'. First, it says A4 'blames the wrong factor', but the app is one of the two joint causes, not an innocent party. Second, it cites the $14,000 fee and the lost funder attendance data (E2, E4, C8). Those are real costs that make A4 worse than A1, but they don't fall under 'worsen outcomes, suppress information or disable a control'. Losing funder reporting data is not suppressing information about the problem. 'Premature' doesn't fit either. A4 does not depend on an unconfirmed hypothesis, because it works under the confirmed H3. That H1 ('app alone') is contradicted doesn't make A4 harmful, since A4 works through H3, not H1. A4 is reasonable but clearly inferior to A1: it is costly, hits all four sites when only two need it, and includes no outreach to lapsed regulars. That is exactly 'acceptable'.
rulings.fix: No fix needed. As optional hardening, add one sentence to C2 or C7 saying the Dock Street and Westgate lead volunteers kept the old paper standing rosters and could run them again. That removes any doubt that A4 would restore slots, and with it any 'premature' or 'harmful' reading.

rulings.explanation: The concern is that commitment level confounds the comparison: perhaps the more committed regulars grabbed slots at the Thursday release, and the less committed lost them and drifted away. The evidence answers this in three ways. (1) Slot loss was set off from outside the volunteers. Pre-booking fell from 74/week to 3/week on 1 May because the coordinator posts were cut (C7). The volunteers' own behaviour did not cause that change. (2) The site-level natural experiment in C2 lines up with it. Millbrook kept pre-booking, only 7 of 117 regulars lost their slot there, and it stayed stable. Collapse happened only at the two sites where pre-booking stopped, and a commitment confound cannot produce that site pattern. (3) The mechanism is confirmed directly: 44 of 61 callbacks say 'lost my regular shift / nobody booked me'. Add the timing (slot loss in May–June came before the lapses), the size of the gap (88% vs 11%), and the main rival being ruled out (121 of 123 lapsed volunteers held current checks), and the evidence meets the bar for 'causal'. 'Association-only' would ignore the exogenous trigger and the site contrast.
rulings.fix: No fix needed. As optional hardening, add a line to C7 saying that before May, regulars who later lost their slot had shift frequency and tenure similar to those who kept it. That closes the commitment-confound reading explicitly.

rulings.explanation: A2 is not framed as a cheap add-on. It makes recognition 'the centrepiece of the retention response, on the premise that low satisfaction is what is driving regulars to leave.' That premise rests on R4, which is only associational: E6 shows a 37% vs 10% gap with no mechanism, the sample is small and self-selected, and slot loss is a plausible common cause. The lowest-scoring item was 'ease of getting the shifts I want'. The established mechanism (C7) points elsewhere. That fits the definition of 'premature' exactly: it could be right if an unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed, but committing to it now is not justified. 'Acceptable' would need the action to be reasonable as stated. Making an unsupported premise the core of the response, in place of the established slot-loss fix, is not reasonable. It isn't 'harmful' either, because recognition activity does no lasting damage.
rulings.fix: No fix needed. The wording 'centrepiece ... on the premise that' already rules out the add-on reading.

rulings.explanation: The concern is that commitment level confounds the comparison: perhaps the more committed regulars grabbed slots at the Thursday release, and the less committed lost them and drifted away. The evidence answers this in three ways. (1) Slot loss was set off from outside the volunteers. Pre-booking fell from 74/week to 3/week on 1 May because the coordinator posts were cut (C7). The volunteers' own behaviour did not cause that change. (2) The site-level natural experiment in C2 lines up with it. Millbrook kept pre-booking, only 7 of 117 regulars lost their slot there, and it stayed stable. Collapse happened only at the two sites where pre-booking stopped, and a commitment confound cannot produce that site pattern. (3) The mechanism is confirmed directly: 44 of 61 callbacks say 'lost my regular shift / nobody booked me'. Add the timing (slot loss in May–June came before the lapses), the size of the gap (88% vs 11%), and the main rival being ruled out (121 of 123 lapsed volunteers held current checks), and the evidence meets the bar for 'causal'. 'Association-only' would ignore the exogenous trigger and the site contrast.
rulings.fix: No fix needed. As optional hardening, add a line to C7 saying that before May, regulars who later lost their slot had shift frequency and tenure similar to those who kept it. That closes the commitment-confound reading explicitly.

rulings.explanation: A2 is not framed as a cheap add-on. It makes recognition 'the centrepiece of the retention response, on the premise that low satisfaction is what is driving regulars to leave.' That premise rests on R4, which is only associational: E6 shows a 37% vs 10% gap with no mechanism, the sample is small and self-selected, and slot loss is a plausible common cause. The lowest-scoring item was 'ease of getting the shifts I want'. The established mechanism (C7) points elsewhere. That fits the definition of 'premature' exactly: it could be right if an unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed, but committing to it now is not justified. 'Acceptable' would need the action to be reasonable as stated. Making an unsupported premise the core of the response, in place of the established slot-loss fix, is not reasonable. It isn't 'harmful' either, because recognition activity does no lasting damage.
rulings.fix: No fix needed. The wording 'centrepiece ... on the premise that' already rules out the add-on reading.
